newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Cavallo sounds warning on Fernandez.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Cavallo sounds warning on Fernandez.

text.p: Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez "doesn't know where he stands" and the package of tax reforms he sent Congress last month is "very dangerous," his predecessor Domingo Cavallo said.

"When I heard of the measures I called him because I was very worried about what his propsals on taxes and how debate was shaping up in Congress," Cavallo told the local magazine Gente in an interview published Thursday.

"I told him than in its present form the tax package was very dangerous, and I suggested that the focus should be on not raising spending and waiting until economic recovery and the fight against tax evasion generate more revenue," he said.

Two weeks after taking office July 29, Fernandez announced a package of tax reforms to plug Argentina's fiscal hole. The measures, still up for debate in Congress, raise taxes on fuels, broaden value-added-tax and scrap business subsidies.

"Creating new and more taxes is a very costly political move," said Cavallo, who launched Argentina's convertibility program in April 1991. The plan, which pegs the dollar and peso at par, tamed runaway inflation and spurred strong growth for four years.
Cavallo said Fernandez "does not know where he stands and lacks good information -- it's very difficult to manage the economy if you don't have good information and know who's who."
Cavallo was sacked by President Carlos Menem after a long string of clashes with members of the ruling Peronist party in Congress and leaders of the party's old guard.

But Fernandez, the former Central Bank chief under Cavallo, inherited 17.1 percent unemployment and a fiscal deficit which he estimated at $6.6 billion (before fiscal reforms) against Cavallo's forecast of $3.5 billion.
Cavallo, in the interview, also repeated his charges of corruption in government circles.

"Mafias are engrained in society's whole power structure and make their way up to the different areas of government," said Cavallo, charging that his attempts to crack these mafias were thwarted by political leaders.
